title: Weighing the wonders by their results
source_text: Ἀλλ᾿ ἐροῦσιν Ἕλληνες ταῦτα μύθους. καίτοι γε μαρτυρούμενα ὡς ἀληθῆ ὑπὸ ὅλων δύο ἐθνῶν. τί δὲ οὐχὶ μᾶλλον τὰ Ἑλλήνων μῦθοι η ταῦτα; εἰ δὲ καὶ ὁμόσε τις χωρήσας τῷ λόγῳ. ἵνα μὴ δόξῃ ἀποκληρωτικῶς τὰ μὲν σφέτερα παραδέχεσθαι τοῖς δ᾿ ἀλλοτρίοις ἀπιστεῖν, φήσαι καὶ τὰ Ἑλλήνων ὑπό τινων γεγονέναι δαιμόνων καὶ τὰ Ἰουδαίων ἤτοι ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ διὰ τῶν προφητῶν ἢ ὑπὸ τῶν ἀγγέλων ἢ ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ διὰ τῶν ἀγγέλων, καὶ τὰ Χριστιανῶν δὲ ὑπὸ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ καὶ τῆς ἐν τοῖς ἀποστόλοις δυνάμεως αὐτοῦ· φέρ᾿ ἅπαντα παραθῶμεν ἀλλήλοις καὶ τὸ τέλος ἴδωμεν τοῦ βουλήματος τῶν ἐνεργησάντων καὶ τὴν ἀπὸ τούτου ὠφέλειαν ἢ βλάβην ἢ οὐδέτερα τῶν τὰς νομιζομένας εὐεργεσίας πεπονθότων, εἰ μὴ φιλόσοφον μὲν ὄψεται τὸ πάλαι Ἰουδαίων ἔθνος, πρὶν ἐξυβρίσωσιν εἰς τὸ θεῖον, ὑφ᾿ οὗ διὰ τὴν πολλὴν κακίαν ἐγκατελείφθησαν, παραδόξως δὲ συστάντας Χριστιανοὺς κατὰ τὴν ἀρχὴν μάλιστα ὑπὸ τῶν τεραστίων ἤπερ τῶν προτρεπτικῶν λόγων προσαγομένους τῷ καταλιπεῖν μὲν τὰ πάτρια αἱρεῖσθαι δὲ τὰ τῶν πατρίων ἀλλότρια. καὶ γὰρ, εἰ χρὴ καὶ τῷ εἰκότι χρῆσθαι λόγῳ περὶ τῆς ἀρχῆθεν Χριστιανῶν συστάσεως, φήσομεν ὅτι οὐ πιθανὸν οὔτε τοὺς Ἰησοῦ ἀποστόλους, ἄνδρας ἀγραμμάτους καὶ ἰδιώτας, ἄλλῳ τινὶ τεθαῤῥηκέναι πρὸς τὸ καταγγεῖλαι τοῖς ἀνθρώποις χριστιανισμὸν ἢ τῇ δοθείσῃ αὐτοῖς δυνάμει καὶ τῇ ἐν τῷ λόγῳ εἰς τὰ δηλούμενα πράγματα χάριτι, ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲ τοὺς ἀκροωμένους αὐτῶν μετατεθεῖσθαι ἐκ πατρίων πολυχρονίων ἐθῶν, μὴ ἀξιολόγου τινὸς δυνάμεως αὐτοὺς καὶ τεραστίων πραγμάτων μετακινησάντων ἐπὶ τὰ οὕτως ξένα καὶ ἀλλότρια τῶν συντρόφων αὐτοῖς δογμάτων.
pass_a_gloss: But Greeks will say (ἐροῦσιν) these are myths (μύθους); and yet testified (μαρτυρούμενα) as true by two whole nations (ἐθνῶν). Why are not rather the Greeks' things myths than these? But if someone, going to close quarters (ὁμόσε χωρήσας) with the argument, so as not to seem arbitrarily/by lot (ἀποκληρωτικῶς) to accept (παραδέχεσθαι) his own but disbelieve (ἀπιστεῖν) others', should say the Greeks' things came about by certain demons (δαιμόνων), and the Jews' either by God through the prophets, or by the angels, or by God through the angels, and the Christians' by Jesus and His power (δύναμις) in the apostles: come, let us set all beside one another (παραθῶμεν) and see the end (τέλος) of the intention (βούλημα) of those who worked them (ἐνεργησάντων) and the benefit (ὠφέλεια) or harm (βλάβη) or neither of those who experienced the reputed benefactions (εὐεργεσίας); whether he will not see the ancient nation of the Jews philosophic (φιλόσοφον), before they committed outrage (ἐξυβρίσωσιν) toward the Divine (τὸ θεῖον), by which because of much wickedness (κακία) they were forsaken (ἐγκατελείφθησαν); and the Christians, having come together unexpectedly (παραδόξως συστάντας), at the beginning especially brought (προσαγομένους) by wonders (τεραστίων) rather than by exhortatory words (προτρεπτικῶν λόγων) to leave ancestral things (τὰ πάτρια) and choose things foreign to the ancestral. For if one must use the argument from likelihood (τῷ εἰκότι λόγῳ) about the original formation (σύστασις) of Christians, we shall say it is not credible (οὐ πιθανόν) that the apostles of Jesus, unlettered (ἀγραμμάτους) and laymen (ἰδιώτας), took courage (τεθαῤῥηκέναι) in anything else to proclaim (καταγγεῖλαι) Christianity to men than the power given them and the grace (χάρις) in the word toward the matters made known; nor that their hearers were changed (μετατεθεῖσθαι) from ancestral long-standing customs (ἐθῶν), unless some notable power and wondrous deeds moved them (μετακινησάντων) to things so strange (ξένα) and foreign to the teachings (δογμάτων) they were raised with (συντρόφων).
pass_b_english: But the Greeks will say that these things are myths, even though two whole nations bear witness that they are true. And why are the stories of the Greeks not myths rather than these? Suppose, however, that someone meets the argument head on, and, so as not to seem to accept his own accounts arbitrarily while disbelieving those of others, says that the Greek wonders too were done by certain demons; the Jewish ones either by God through the prophets, or by the angels, or by God through the angels; and the Christian ones by Jesus and by His power at work in the apostles. Come, then, let us set them all side by side and look at the end that those who worked them had in view, and at the benefit or harm, or neither, that came of it to those who received what were thought to be benefits.

Will such a person not see that the Jewish nation of old was a nation of philosophers, before they behaved outrageously toward the Divine, by whom they were forsaken because of their great wickedness; and that the Christians, who came together against all expectation, were drawn at the beginning more by wonders than by words of exhortation to abandon their ancestral ways and to choose ways foreign to those of their fathers? For if we must also use the argument from likelihood about how the Christians first came together, we shall say that it is not credible that the apostles of Jesus, unlettered and ordinary men (Acts 4:13), took courage to proclaim Christianity to men from anything other than the power given to them and the grace in their word for setting forth the things it proclaimed; nor is it credible that those who heard them were moved from long-standing ancestral customs, unless some remarkable power and wondrous deeds had moved them toward teachings so strange and so foreign to those they had been brought up with.

choices.choice: ‘Two whole nations’ = Jews and Christians, both testifying to the Old Testament wonders listed in 8.46. καὶ τὰ Ἑλλήνων ... γεγονέναι: the hypothetical speaker concedes that the Greek wonders really happened and assigns them to demons; ‘too’ keeps that concession. τὸ θεῖον is neuter; rendered ‘the Divine, by whom’ to keep the agency of the forsaking with God. εἰ μὴ ... ὄψεται depends loosely on ἴδωμεν (‘let us see whether he will not see’); rendered as a direct question, with ‘such a person’ naming the τις of the earlier clause. The phrase τῇ ἐν τῷ λόγῳ εἰς τὰ δηλούμενα πράγματα χάριτι is compressed: ‘the grace in their word for setting forth the things it proclaimed’ takes εἰς τὰ δηλούμενα as the grace’s bearing on the matters made known. ἀγραμμάτους καὶ ἰδιώτας echoes Acts 4:13 (ἀγράμματοί εἰσιν καὶ ἰδιῶται) and is cited inline.
Title changed: 'by Their Fruit' echoed Matthew 7:16, which the chapter does not use; Origen weighs the end and the benefit or harm
Added 'too' for καί in καὶ τὰ Ἑλλήνων (the speaker concedes the Greek wonders happened)
'Will he not see' -> 'Will such a person not see' so the subject (τις) is clear after the intervening exhortation
'the grace in their word that made its message plain' -> 'the grace in their word for setting forth the things it proclaimed' (removed added 'made plain'; δηλούμενα = things made known)
Acts 4:13 verified against ἀγράμματοί εἰσιν καὶ ἰδιῶται

anf_compare.notes: Crombie (ANF 1872) and Chadwick (1953) were not used or consulted; the English is from the Greek.
